question: Under what circumstances can delay in lodging an FIR prove fatal to prosecution?
generated_answer: Mere delay in lodging or registering an FIR is not a ground for quashing the FIR itself (*Shento Varghese v. Julfikar Husen & Ors.* [2024] 6 S.C.R. 409). Similarly, a delay in forwarding the FIR to the jurisdictional magistrate is not fatal to the prosecution case, and mere delay by itself is insufficient to discard or disbelieve the prosecution (*Rama Devi v. The State of Bihar and Others* [2024] 10 S.C.R. 1313). When an accused raises a specific contention regarding such delay, they must demonstrate how the delay has prejudiced their case (*Rama Devi v. The State of Bihar and Others* [2024] 10 S.C.R. 1313; *Shento Varghese v. Julfikar Husen & Ors.* [2024] 6 S.C.R. 409). Unless serious prejudice is demonstrated to have been suffered by the accused and the prosecution fails to explain the delay, the delay does not have a deteriorating effect on the prosecution case (*Shento Varghese v. Julfikar Husen & Ors.* [2024] 6 S.C.R. 409). If prejudice is demonstrated and the prosecution fails to provide an explanation, the utmost effect of the delay is to render the date and time of lodging the FIR suspect (*Shento Varghese v. Julfikar Husen & Ors.* [2024] 6 S.C.R. 409). Conversely, if the investigation starts in right earnest, there is sufficient material showing that the accused were named and pinpointed, and the court finds the witnesses to be truthful and credible, the lack of a cogent explanation for the delay is not regarded as detrimental (*Rama Devi v. The State of Bihar and Others* [2024] 10 S.C.R. 1313).

question: Can a conviction be sustained solely on the testimony of a single eyewitness?
generated_answer: A conviction can be based solely on the testimony of a solitary or single witness, provided that such testimony is found to be credible, trustworthy, and critically examined (*George v. The State of Tamil Nadu and Others*, [2024] 12 S.C.R. 769; *Vishwajeet Kerba Masalkar v. State of Maharashtra*, [2024] 10 S.C.R. 753). However, the testimony of a solitary witness must inspire confidence in the mind of the court, and where such testimony is found to be unreliable or unconvincing upon deeper scrutiny, a conviction cannot be sustained solely upon it (*Vishwajeet Kerba Masalkar v. State of Maharashtra*, [2024] 10 S.C.R. 753). Furthermore, if the sole witness is an interested witness, their testimony is not to be discarded merely on that ground, but it must be scrutinized with greater caution and circumspection (*George v. The State of Tamil Nadu and Others*, [2024] 12 S.C.R. 769).

question: When may a court interfere with an arbitral award on the ground of public policy?
generated_answer: A court may interfere with an arbitral award on the ground that it is in conflict with the public policy of India only if the making of the award was induced or affected by fraud or corruption or was in violation of section 75 or section 81, if it is in contravention with the fundamental policy of Indian law, or if it is in conflict with the most basic notions of morality or justice (*OPG Power Generation Private Limited v. Enexio Power Cooling Solutions India Private Limited & Anr.*, [2024] 9 S.C.R. 490). The test for determining whether there is a contravention with the fundamental policy of Indian law shall not entail a review on the merits of the dispute (*OPG Power Generation Private Limited v. Enexio Power Cooling Solutions India Private Limited & Anr.*, [2024] 9 S.C.R. 490).

question: What are the conditions for granting anticipatory bail under Indian law?
generated_answer:
Under Indian law, when considering an application for anticipatory bail, courts are generally guided by considerations such as the nature and gravity of the offences, the role attributed to the applicant, and the facts of the case (*Dhanraj Aswani v. Amar S. Mulchandani & Anr.*, [2024] 9 S.C.R. 257). An application for anticipatory bail must be based on concrete facts rather than vague or general allegations, though it is not essential that an application be moved only after an FIR is filed (*Dhanraj Aswani v. Amar S. Mulchandani & Anr.*, [2024] 9 S.C.R. 257). Furthermore, an order granting anticipatory bail can be passed only upon hearing the Public Prosecutor (*Dhanraj Aswani v. Amar S. Mulchandani & Anr.*, [2024] 9 S.C.R. 257). 

Section 438 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC) does not compel or oblige courts to impose conditions limiting relief in terms of time, but courts are justified and ought to impose conditions spelt out in Section 437(3) of the CrPC by virtue of Section 438(2), while the need for other restrictive conditions must be judged on a case-to-case basis (*Dhanraj Aswani v. Amar S. Mulchandani & Anr.*, [2024] 9 S.C.R. 257). An order of anticipatory bail must not be a "blanket" order and must be confined to a specific incident, and it does not limit the rights of the police to conduct an investigation (*Dhanraj Aswani v. Amar S. Mulchandani & Anr.*, [2024] 9 S.C.R. 257). Additionally, where a person has a reasonable apprehension of arrest on an accusation of committing a non-bailable offence, they may apply to the High Court or the Court of Session for a direction that they be released on bail in the event of arrest (*Shajan Skaria v. The State of Kerala & Anr.*, [2024] 8 S.C.R. 1086).

question: Under what circumstances can a court permit amendment of pleadings after the commencement of trial, and what factors should guide the exercise of its judicial discretion?
generated_answer:
Under Order VI Rule 17 of the C.P.C., an application for the amendment of pleadings after the commencement of trial cannot be allowed unless the court concludes that, despite due diligence, the party could not have raised the matter before the trial commenced. The burden of proof rests entirely on the party seeking the amendment post-commencement to demonstrate that it could not have been sought earlier despite due diligence, as such amendments cannot be claimed as a matter of right under all circumstances (*Basavaraj v. Indira and Others*, [2024] 2 S.C.R. 935). 

In exercising its judicial discretion, a court may refuse leave to amend if the application introduces a totally different, new, and inconsistent case, or alters the fundamental character of the suit (*Basavaraj v. Indira and Others*, [2024] 2 S.C.R. 935). Although amendments are normally permitted to avoid multiplicity of litigation, the court must consider whether the application is bona fide or mala fide, and whether the proposed amendment would cause prejudice to the opposing side that cannot be adequately compensated in monetary terms (*Basavaraj v. Indira and Others*, [2024] 2 S.C.R. 935). Vague grounds such as oversight or mistake, when facts were already within the knowledge of the party, do not constitute sufficient compliance with the due diligence requirement to warrant allowing an amendment at the fag end of a trial (*Basavaraj v. Indira and Others*, [2024] 2 S.C.R. 935).

question: What are the essential ingredients required to establish criminal conspiracy, and what kind of circumstantial evidence is legally sufficient to prove an unlawful agreement between the accused persons?
generated_answer:
The essential ingredient and *sine qua non* for the offence of criminal conspiracy under Sections 120A and 120B of the IPC is an agreement between two or more persons to commit an offence, or to do an illegal act (or a legal act through illegal means). The offence is complete as soon as there is a meeting of minds or *consensus ad idem* regarding the design or object of the conspiracy, and whether or not the offence is actually committed is immaterial. 

Regarding the proof of such an agreement, because criminal conspiracies are hatched in privacy, it would rarely be possible to establish them by direct evidence. Furthermore, relying on a few scattered bits of evidence is not sufficient to connect an accused to the crime of criminal conspiracy.

question: Can an authorised signatory be convicted under the penal provisions governing company offences solely because he signed documents on the company's behalf?
generated_answer: Under corporate law, authorised signatories act on behalf of the company and can bind the company through their actions, but they do not assume the company's legal identity or merge their legal status with it (*BIJOY KUMAR MONI v. PARESH MANNA & ANR.*, [2024] 12 S.C.R. 1946). In the context of statutory offences such as those under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, the provision contemplates only the drawer of the cheque to be responsible for the commission of the offence, and an authorised signatory who merely signs a cheque on behalf of the company does not become the drawer (*BIJOY KUMAR MONI v. PARESH MANNA & ANR.*, [2024] 12 S.C.R. 1946; *BIJAY AGARWAL v. M/S MEDILINES*, [2024] 10 S.C.R. 1890). Certain persons other than the drawer can be made liable only by virtue of specific statutory provisions (such as Section 141) extending liability in cases where the offence is committed by a company (*BIJOY KUMAR MONI v. PARESH MANNA & ANR.*, [2024] 12 S.C.R. 1946). Furthermore, penal statutes must be interpreted strictly when determining liability and vicarious liability (*BIJAY AGARWAL v. M/S MEDILINES*, [2024] 10 S.C.R. 1890).
